title: five who said yes
hookLine: the five people dressed alike at the front of the parade, and the day in 1699 they stand in for

lines: FIVE, DRESSED ALIKE, AT THE FRONT.
cards: At the front of a Sikh parade, ahead of the float carrying the scripture, walk five people dressed alike, swords held upright. They aren't security, and they aren't there for show.
They're standing in for five people from more than three hundred years ago, who did something nobody in the crowd that day expected.

teach.b: Spring, 1699, at Anandpur in the hills of Punjab. A huge crowd has gathered for the harvest festival, Vaisakhi.
The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, walks out with a drawn sword and asks a question that silences everyone: who will give their head for the faith? One man stands, Daya Ram.
The Guru takes him into a tent and comes back out alone. Then he asks again. Four more stand, one at a time.
What happened inside that tent, the tellings differ.
What they agree on is what came next: all five walked out alive, dressed alike, beside the Guru.

teach.h: FIVE CASTES, FIVE CORNERS OF INDIA.
teach.b: They're remembered as the Panj Pyare: panj, five, pyare, beloved. And look who they were. A shopkeeper from Lahore.
A farmer from near Delhi. A water-carrier from Puri, on the eastern coast. A cloth printer from Dwarka, in the far west.

A barber from Bidar, in the south. Castes that, around them, would never have shared a meal, from homes a thousand miles apart. They became the first of the Khalsa, the community of committed Sikhs: one family.
The men took one name, Singh, lion, and Sikh women carry the name Kaur. Two names that rank no one.

how: At every amrit initiation, five initiated Sikhs stand in as the Panj Pyare, and five Sikhs dressed alike lead Nagar Kirtan processions ahead of the Guru Granth Sahib; the Khalsa's founding is celebrated every year at Vaisakhi.

games.q: who's who, and what's what — tap the pairs.
p: two names that rank no one

s: the five who stood up all came from the same caste
a shopkeeper, a farmer, a water-carrier, a cloth printer and a barber, from across India.
all five walked out of the tent alive
the tellings differ about the tent, but all five came out, dressed alike, beside the Guru.
five Sikhs still stand in for the Panj Pyare today
at every initiation, and at the head of processions.

games.q: you're the tenth Guru. five people from five different castes have just stood up for the faith. what do you do with them?
o: rank them by family, highest first.
dress them alike and make them one family.
games.why: they became the first of the Khalsa, one family with one name: Singh.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, picture the crowd on the hillside, gone quiet. On the second, picture one person standing up when nobody else will.
On the third, sit a little taller yourself, the way someone does when they stand for what they love.

wordCard.voice: Panj Pyare. The five beloved: strangers from across India who stood up, and walked out one family. Fourth word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: panj (five) + pyare (beloved ones).

carryVoice: Your line: five strangers, one family. The five at the front of every parade are standing in for them. That's day four.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition of the Vaisakhi of 1699 at Anandpur (the call, the five, the first amrit)
the Panj Pyare: Bhai Daya Singh (Lahore), Bhai Dharam Singh (Hastinapur, near Delhi), Bhai Himmat Singh (Jagannath Puri), Bhai Mohkam Singh (Dwarka), Bhai Sahib Singh (Bidar)
Sikh Rehat Maryada (the Panj Pyare at amrit initiation; the names Singh and Kaur)
'vah vah Gobind Singh aape gur chela' (var attributed to Bhai Gurdas II)
